MUQATIL:59:18/r1.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:59:18/r1.speaker: author
MUQATIL:59:18/r1.claim: Believers are warned against alliance with Jews and told to review what they have prepared for the Day of Resurrection.

MUQATIL:59:18/r2.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:59:18/r2.speaker: author
MUQATIL:59:18/r2.claim: Fear God again; He knows good and evil deeds, including assistance to Jews, and believers should not abandon His command or become like the People of the Book.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p285/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p285/r1.speaker: قتادة
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p285/r1.claim: Qatada explains what a person has sent ahead for tomorrow as what they send ahead for Judgment Day.

TUSTARI:59:18/r1.author: Sahl al-Tustarī
TUSTARI:59:18/r1.speaker: author
TUSTARI:59:18/r1.claim: God asks a servant about duties owed to the self, to the knowledge between the servant and God, and to the intellect; one should fulfill these through careful attention to the outcome.

TUSTARI:59:18/r2.author: Sahl al-Tustarī
TUSTARI:59:18/r2.speaker: الحسن
TUSTARI:59:18/r2.claim: Al-Hasan says that at a person’s death other people ask what he left behind, while the angels ask what he sent ahead.

TAB-FULL:v22p547/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v22p547/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v22p547/r1.claim: Believers must fulfill God's obligations and avoid disobedience, then examine what deeds they sent ahead for Resurrection: saving good deeds or ruinous bad ones.

TAB-FULL:v22p547/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v22p547/r2.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v22p547/r2.claim: Qatāda says God made the Hour feel near by describing it as tomorrow, the Day of Resurrection.

TAB-FULL:v22p547/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v22p547/r3.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v22p547/r3.claim: Qatāda glosses “tomorrow” as the Day of Resurrection.

TAB-FULL:v22p547/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v22p547/r4.speaker: الضحاك
TAB-FULL:v22p547/r4.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk likewise says “tomorrow” means the Day of Resurrection.

TAB-FULL:v22p547/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v22p547/r5.speaker: ابن زيد
TAB-FULL:v22p547/r5.claim: Ibn Zayd says one should consider good and evil for the afterlife; yesterday denotes worldly life and tomorrow the afterlife, as in the image of a town gone by yesterday.

ZAJJAJ:v5p149/r3.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v5p149/r3.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v5p149/r3.claim: “Tomorrow” means Judgment Day, brought close to people as though it were tomorrow; ghadan derives from ghaduww, normally written without the wāw in Quranic usage.

ZAJJAJ:v5p149/r4.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v5p149/r4.speaker: الشاعر
ZAJJAJ:v5p149/r4.claim: An unnamed poet retains the wāw in ghaduww, using ghaduwwan to mean a barren place the next day.

ZAJJAJ:v5p149/r5.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v5p149/r5.speaker: آخر
ZAJJAJ:v5p149/r5.claim: A second, unnamed poet also retains the wāw in ghaduww.

NAHHAS:v4p402/r1.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v4p402/r1.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v4p402/r1.claim: Piety means performing obligations and avoiding sins; the imperative's kasra is omitted because it is heavy beside the attached wāw.

NAHHAS:v4p402/r2.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v4p402/r2.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v4p402/r2.claim: Each soul should examine what it sent ahead for Judgment Day: good that saves or evil that ruins it; ghadan derives from ghaduw.

NAHHAS:v4p402/r3.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v4p402/r3.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v4p402/r3.claim: Repeating the command to fear God emphasizes the admonition.

SULAMI:v2p320#3/r1.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v2p320#3/r1.speaker: أبو عثمان
SULAMI:v2p320#3/r1.claim: Whoever reflects on tomorrow attends to today more carefully; whoever neglects tomorrow wastes the moments and hours of the present.

SULAMI:v2p320#3/r2.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v2p320#3/r2.speaker: بعضهم
SULAMI:v2p320#3/r2.claim: The pious focus on their end and tomorrow, while people of spiritual realities focus on their lot and pre-eternal beginning; both paths are sound, and the loser neglects both.

THALABI:v9p286/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v9p286/r4.speaker: author
THALABI:v9p286/r4.claim: Piety means performing obligations and avoiding sins; each person should consider what good he has sent ahead for the Resurrection.

MAWARDI-FULL:v5p510/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p510/r1.speaker: معن أو عون عن ابن مسعود
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p510/r1.claim: Ibn Masud told a man seeking counsel to listen when God addresses believers, since it commands good or prohibits evil.

MAWARDI-FULL:v5p510/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p510/r2.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p510/r2.claim: Fear of God may mean avoiding hypocrites or doubtful matters.

MAWARDI-FULL:v5p510/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p510/r3.speaker: ابن زيد
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p510/r3.claim: Each soul should consider the good or evil it has sent ahead.

MAWARDI-FULL:v5p510/r4.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p510/r4.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p510/r4.claim: Tomorrow means Resurrection; yesterday means this world.

MAWARDI-FULL:v5p510/r5.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p510/r5.speaker: قتادة
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p510/r5.claim: God calls the Hour tomorrow to make its arrival seem near.

MAWARDI-FULL:v5p510/r6.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p510/r6.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p510/r6.claim: Repeated fear may confirm the first command or distinguish repentance for past sins from avoiding future sins.

MAWARDI-FULL:v5p510/r7.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p510/r7.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p510/r7.claim: Alternatively, the first concerns deeds sent ahead for tomorrow and the second future conduct.

MAWARDI-FULL:v5p510/r8.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p510/r8.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p510/r8.claim: God knows deeds, or people and what they will do.

QUSHAYRI:v3p306/r5.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v3p306/r5.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v3p306/r5.claim: The first command to fear God means remembering punishment and reflecting on deeds; the second means vigilant self-accounting.

QUSHAYRI:v3p306/r6.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v3p306/r6.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v3p306/r6.claim: Those who neither audit deeds nor watch spiritual states will soon be exposed; concern for tomorrow is shown by attending well to today and reflecting on yesterday.

QUSHAYRI:v3p306/r7.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v3p306/r7.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v3p306/r7.claim: Some reflect on what was decreed from eternity, some on tomorrow, and others devote themselves to the present obligation, immersed in God beyond past and future.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p391/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p391/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p391/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas says people should examine the deeds they have sent ahead, considering their reward or punishment and whether they are good or ruinous.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p391/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p391/r2.speaker: ابن إسحاق
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p391/r2.claim: Ibn Ishaq says tomorrow means the Resurrection; it is called tomorrow to make it feel near, and the syntax means for tomorrow.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:59:15-18/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:59:15-18/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:59:15-18/r4.claim: Believers should fulfill obligations, avoid sins, and consider the righteous deeds sent ahead for Resurrection Day.

JISHUMI:v9p6861/r12.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v9p6861/r12.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v9p6861/r12.claim: The verse requires reflection, self-accounting, and preparation for the Day of Resurrection.

JISHUMI:v9p6861/r3.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v9p6861/r3.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v9p6861/r3.claim: God-consciousness means protecting oneself from punishment by performing obligations and avoiding sins.

JISHUMI:v9p6861/r4.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v9p6861/r4.speaker: قتادة والضحاك وابن زيد
JISHUMI:v9p6861/r4.claim: They interpret tomorrow as the Day of Resurrection.

JISHUMI:v9p6861/r5.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v9p6861/r5.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v9p6861/r5.claim: The repeated command to be mindful may concern future conduct followed by repentance for past conduct, may be emphasis, or may address everyone first and then direct each person to self-examination.

JISHUMI:v9p6861/r6.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v9p6861/r6.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v9p6861/r6.claim: Looking ahead means taking account of oneself and what one has prepared for the gathering; calling the Resurrection tomorrow signals its nearness, as Qatada says.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p86/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p86/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p86/r1.claim: “Tomorrow” means resurrection; each person should examine what he has sent ahead, righteous deeds that save or bad deeds that ruin.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p290#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p290#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p290#2/r1.claim: This is admonition about the afterlife and a warning from God, from whom nothing is hidden.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p290#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p290#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p290#2/r2.claim: Most read wa-l-tanẓur with a silent lām and jussive rāʾ; another group uses kasra on the imperative lām; al-Ḥasan reads the rāʾ in the subjunctive, expressing purpose after the command to fear God.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p290#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p290#2/r3.speaker: قتادة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p290#2/r3.claim: Lighad means Resurrection Day; Qatada says God calls it tomorrow to make it seem near because it will certainly come, while another view takes it as the day of death.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p290#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p290#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p290#2/r4.claim: A person should review past deeds, increase good works, and stop doing wrong.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p290#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p290#2/r5.speaker: مجاهد وابن زيد
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p290#2/r5.claim: Mujāhid and Ibn Zayd say yesterday refers to this world and tomorrow to the afterlife.

TABRISI:59:16-18/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:59:16-18/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:59:16-18/r1.claim: The Quran's ‘tomorrow’ is the Day of Resurrection; each person should inspect what they sent ahead, good deeds that save or bad deeds that ruin them.

TABRISI:59:16-18/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:59:16-18/r2.speaker: قتادة
TABRISI:59:16-18/r2.claim: God made the Hour seem as near as tomorrow to prompt reflection on what people have prepared.

TABRISI:59:16-18/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:59:16-18/r3.speaker: author
TABRISI:59:16-18/r3.claim: The word ghad is originally ghadw, but the Quran always omits its wāw; poetry shows both the omitted and retained forms.

TABRISI:59:16-18/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:59:16-18/r4.speaker: شاعر غير مسمى
TABRISI:59:16-18/r4.claim: The line about people being like dwellings witnesses poetic use of ghad without the wāw.

TABRISI:59:16-18/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:59:16-18/r5.speaker: شاعر غير مسمى
TABRISI:59:16-18/r5.claim: The line urging not to drive a camel and lower a bucket witnesses poetic use of ghad with the wāw.

TABRISI:59:18-20/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:59:18-20/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:59:18-20/r1.claim: The first command to fear God urges repentance for past sins; the second guards against future sins.

TABRISI:59:18-20/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:59:18-20/r2.speaker: author
TABRISI:59:18-20/r2.claim: Alternatively, the repeated command to fear God simply reinforces the first.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p224/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p224/r1.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p224/r1.claim: Each person should examine what they have sent ahead: a righteous deed that saves or an evil deed that ruins.

RAZI-FULL:v29p253#3/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v29p253#3/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v29p253#3/r1.claim: Ghadan means the Resurrection, named 'tomorrow' to make it feel near as the day after today.

RAZI-FULL:v29p253#3/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v29p253#3/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v29p253#3/r2.claim: The indefinite nafs stresses each individual soul's responsibility to examine what it sent ahead.

RAZI-FULL:v29p253#3/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v29p253#3/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v29p253#3/r3.claim: The indefinite 'tomorrow' magnifies and obscures the Day of Resurrection, whose true nature is beyond comprehension.

RAZI-FULL:v29p253#3/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v29p253#3/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v29p253#3/r4.claim: Repeating the command to fear God either reinforces it or assigns the first command to fulfilling duties and the second to avoiding sins.

QURTUBI-FULL:59:18/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:59:18/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:59:18/r1.claim: Fearing God means obeying His commands and prohibitions, fulfilling obligations, and avoiding sins.

QURTUBI-FULL:59:18/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:59:18/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:59:18/r2.claim: Each person should examine what good or evil they have sent ahead for the future, here meaning Resurrection Day; Arabs call the future tomorrow.

QURTUBI-FULL:59:18/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:59:18/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:59:18/r3.claim: A poet says tomorrow is near for those awaiting it; Ḥasan and Qatāda explain that the Hour is made as near as tomorrow, since whatever is coming and certain death are near.

QURTUBI-FULL:59:18/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:59:18/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:59:18/r4.claim: The repeated command to fear God can be emphatic, like repeating “hurry” or “shoot.”

QURTUBI-FULL:59:18/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:59:18/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:59:18/r5.claim: Alternatively, the first command calls for repentance of past sins and the second for avoiding future sins.

QURTUBI-FULL:59:18/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:59:18/r6.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
QURTUBI-FULL:59:18/r6.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr glosses God's being fully aware as knowing what will come from people.

BAYDAWI-FULL:59:18-19/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:59:18-19/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:59:18-19/r1.claim: غد means Judgment Day because it is near or because worldly life is like today and the afterlife tomorrow; its indefinite form magnifies it, while نفس stresses even one individual’s self-examination.

BAYDAWI-FULL:59:18-19/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:59:18-19/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:59:18-19/r2.claim: The repeated command to fear God emphasizes the first duty of performing obligations and the second of avoiding prohibitions; God’s knowledge of acts is a threat for sins.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p234/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p234/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p234/r1.claim: Believers should fear God by obeying His commands and not opposing them.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p234/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p234/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p234/r2.claim: The indefinite “a soul” narrows the number who examine what they sent ahead for the afterlife.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p234/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p234/r3.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p234/r3.claim: “Tomorrow” means Judgment Day, bringing it near, or figures the afterlife as tomorrow after the world's today; its indefinite form magnifies its unknown greatness.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p234/r4.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p234/r4.speaker: مالك بن دينار
NASAFI-FULL:v4p234/r4.claim: Mālik ibn Dīnār reports words written at Paradise's gate: what was done was profit, what was sent ahead was gained, and what was left behind was loss.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p234/r5.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p234/r5.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p234/r5.claim: The repeated command to fear God emphasizes it: the first concerns duties and the second avoiding sins; awareness of God's scrutiny encourages vigilance.

QASHANI:59:18/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:59:18/r1.speaker: author
QASHANI:59:18/r1.claim: For conventional, inherited faith, piety means avoiding sins and acquiring good deeds for after death, while guarding against veiling by desires; God judges acts and intentions according to each person’s intention.

QASHANI:59:18/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:59:18/r2.speaker: author
QASHANI:59:18/r2.claim: Alternatively, realized faith requires avoiding veils caused by one’s own acts and qualities, assessing even minor deeds and traits as rejected barriers.

QASHANI:59:18/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:59:18/r3.speaker: author
QASHANI:59:18/r3.claim: The realized seeker must guard against remnants of selfhood and changing states; God knows both what people do through their selves and what they do without self-assertion.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p148/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p148/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p148/r1.claim: After describing hypocrites and Jews, God admonishes believers; admonition after calamity affects softened hearts and warns against causes of punishment.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p148/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p148/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p148/r2.claim: The repeated command to fear God either reinforces the first or distinguishes performing obligations from avoiding sins under threat.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p148/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p148/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p148/r3.claim: Most read ولتنظر as an imperative; several read the lām with kasra, and al-Ḥasan makes it a purpose lām.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p148/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p148/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p148/r4.claim: The certain Resurrection is called tomorrow to bring it near; other views make tomorrow the afterlife or day of death, and Mujāhid and Ibn Zayd say yesterday is this world.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p148/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p148/r5.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p148/r5.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says the indefinite نفس stresses each soul’s need to consider what it sent ahead for a tremendous, unknowable tomorrow.

SAMIN-DURR:59:18/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:59:18/r1.speaker: العامة
SAMIN-DURR:59:18/r1.claim: The common ولتنظر uses a jussive imperative lām with sukūn; Abu Haywa and Yahya ibn al-Harith use the original kasra.

SAMIN-DURR:59:18/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:59:18/r2.speaker: الحسن
SAMIN-DURR:59:18/r2.claim: Al-Hasan uses kasra with an accusative verb, treating the lām as purposive and supplying an implicit reason.

SAMIN-DURR:59:18/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:59:18/r3.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:59:18/r3.claim: Al-Zamakhshari explains the indefinite نفس as a single soul, stressing how few examine what they have sent ahead, and indefinite غد as great and unknowable.

SAMIN-DURR:59:18/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:59:18/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:59:18/r4.claim: The repeated واتقوا الله may be emphatic, or the first may concern duties and the second avoiding sins, as al-Zamakhshari explains.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p76#2/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p76#2/r1.speaker: أبيه
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p76#2/r1.claim: When impoverished barefoot people arrived, the Prophet urged charity, even half a date; an Ansari brought a large bundle and others followed. He said the initiator of a good or bad practice bears its reward or burden and that of later imitators; Muslim alone transmits this route.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p76#2/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p76#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p76#2/r2.claim: The command to fear God includes doing what He commands and leaving what He forbids.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p77/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p77/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p77/r1.claim: Believers should take account of themselves before being judged and prepare righteous deeds for the Resurrection and presentation before God.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p77/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p77/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p77/r2.claim: The repeated command to fear God reinforces the warning that God knows every act and state, large or small.

BIQAI-FULL:v7p534/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v7p534/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v7p534/r1.claim: After recounting betrayals and false profession, the surah’s warning to believers has special force because admonition after calamity reaches the heart.

BIQAI-FULL:v7p534/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v7p534/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v7p534/r2.claim: Believers must keep God’s limits and guard themselves from punishment for neglecting His commands and prohibitions.

BIQAI-FULL:v7p534/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v7p534/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v7p534/r3.claim: Every self should examine what it has prepared for the coming reckoning; the singular wording also suggests few heed this self-assessment.

BIQAI-FULL:v7p534/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v7p534/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v7p534/r4.claim: “Tomorrow” means the presentation after death or Judgment Day; it is near because death can arrive at any moment, and its indefinite form magnifies it.

BIQAI-FULL:v7p534/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v7p534/r5.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v7p534/r5.claim: The first command to be mindful of God shapes outward deeds; the repeated command calls for inward self-review and purification from subtle satanic corruption.

BIQAI-FULL:v7p534/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v7p534/r6.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v7p534/r6.claim: God fully knows visible and hidden deeds, so the repetition of His name emphasizes that His encompassing awareness applies to every state.

DURR-FULL:v8p119/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p119/r4.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
DURR-FULL:v8p119/r4.claim: After seeing needy people from Mudar, the Prophet recited the warning to remember tomorrow, urged charity before it became impossible, and taught that whoever starts a good or bad practice shares its reward or burden; the community gave and he distributed it.

DURR-FULL:v8p120/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p120/r1.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v8p120/r1.claim: Qatada says what a person sends ahead for tomorrow means the Day of Resurrection.

DURR-FULL:v8p120/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p120/r2.speaker: أبو بكر الصديق
DURR-FULL:v8p120/r2.claim: Abu Bakr's sermon warns that lifespans are hidden and urges people to remain wary, recalling that those who forget God are made to forget themselves.

BURSEVI:v9p362#2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p362#2/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v9p362#2/r1.claim: Repeating ‘fear God’ emphasizes taqwā and that each matter should begin and end with it; one reading makes the first command performance of duties and the second avoidance of prohibitions.

BURSEVI:v9p362#2/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p362#2/r2.speaker: كشف الأسرار
BURSEVI:v9p362#2/r2.claim: Another interpretation makes the first taqwā its root and the second its completion, or distinguishes ordinary avoidance of prohibitions from the elect’s avoidance of everything besides God.

BURSEVI:v9p362#2/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p362#2/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v9p362#2/r3.claim: Taqwā is avoiding whatever incurs sin by action or omission; some masters distinguish protection from harmful deeds, attributes, and finally everything besides God.

BURSEVI:v9p362#2/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p362#2/r4.speaker: عزيزي
BURSEVI:v9p362#2/r4.claim: The world is like pottery seen in sleep, while the hereafter is a jewel found awake; true piety responds to the jewel found in wakefulness.

BURSEVI:v9p362#2/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p362#2/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v9p362#2/r5.claim: Taqwā must accompany action; a Persian verse by Sāʾib links it to work rather than mere claims.

BURSEVI:v9p362#2/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p362#2/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v9p362#2/r6.claim: A report says that after a person dies, people ask what he left behind while angels ask what he sent ahead; an inscription at Paradise says entrants profited from what they sent ahead.

BURSEVI:v9p362#2/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p362#2/r7.speaker: مالك بن دينار
BURSEVI:v9p362#2/r7.claim: Saʿdūn tells Mālik ibn Dīnār that the afterlife journey is long and dangerous; he mourns days spent without good deeds and says love of God, not madness, overwhelms him.

BURSEVI:v9p362/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p362/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v9p362/r1.claim: Taqwā covers actions and omissions: obey rather than disobey, show gratitude rather than ingratitude, remember rather than forget, and witness God’s acts rather than be veiled by one’s own.

BURSEVI:v9p362/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p362/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v9p362/r2.claim: The conditional ‘what’ asks each person to examine what deeds they sent ahead for Resurrection; good deeds call for gratitude and increase, sins for repentance and regret.

BURSEVI:v9p362/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p362/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v9p362/r3.claim: The hereafter is called ‘tomorrow’ because it is near; alternatively, worldly time is like a day and the hereafter its morrow because their conditions correspond and the second follows the first.

BURSEVI:v9p362/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p362/r4.speaker: الحسن
BURSEVI:v9p362/r4.claim: Al-Ḥasan says God continually brought the hereafter nearer in the wording until He made it like tomorrow.

BURSEVI:v9p362/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p362/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v9p362/r5.claim: The hereafter is like tomorrow because people are asleep in worldly life and awaken at death; death and Resurrection are morning to the heedless, making this world dark and the next luminous.

BURSEVI:v9p362/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p362/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v9p362/r6.claim: The indefinite ‘tomorrow’ magnifies an unknowable day; its original form had a wāw, preserved in Labīd’s cited verse.

BURSEVI:v9p362/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p362/r7.speaker: لبيد
BURSEVI:v9p362/r7.claim: Labīd’s verse about people and ruined dwellings is cited as evidence for the original form ghadu and as a poem of reflection.

BURSEVI:v9p362/r8.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p362/r8.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v9p362/r8.claim: Making ‘soul’ indefinite stresses each person’s responsibility to examine alone what they sent ahead; ‘independence’ can mean counting souls as few or examining deeds without another’s view.

ALUSI-FULL:v28p60/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v28p60/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v28p60/r1.claim: Taqwā covers everything one does and leaves undone.

ALUSI-FULL:v28p60/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v28p60/r10.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v28p60/r10.claim: Another view says taqwā already includes avoiding sin, so there is no basis to divide the two commands and emphasis better fits the passage; al-Ālūsī objects that the preceding phrase naturally suggests good deeds and finally leans toward distinction.

ALUSI-FULL:v28p60/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v28p60/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v28p60/r2.claim: “Tomorrow” means Resurrection because it is near as tomorrow is to yesterday, or because worldly life is like a day before the distinct conditions of the next life; its indefiniteness magnifies an unknowable, tremendous day.

ALUSI-FULL:v28p60/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v28p60/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v28p60/r3.claim: The indefinite nafs minimizes the number who truly examine their deeds, strengthening the exhortation and censuring widespread heedlessness.

ALUSI-FULL:v28p60/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v28p60/r4.speaker: الكشف
ALUSI-FULL:v28p60/r4.claim: Al-Kashf says the command to examine is broad, but those who actually comply are exceedingly few; it cites a report comparing people to a hundred camels with scarcely one fit mount.

ALUSI-FULL:v28p60/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v28p60/r5.speaker: ابن عطية
ALUSI-FULL:v28p60/r5.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya suggests that “tomorrow” means the day after death; al-Ālūsī says this is weak.

ALUSI-FULL:v28p60/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v28p60/r6.speaker: أبو حيوة، يحيى بن الحارث، حفص
ALUSI-FULL:v28p60/r6.claim: Abū Ḥaywa, Yaḥyā ibn al-Ḥārith, and Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim read li-tanẓur with a kasra on the lām.

ALUSI-FULL:v28p60/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v28p60/r7.speaker: الحسن
ALUSI-FULL:v28p60/r7.claim: Al-Ḥasan reads the lām with kasra and the rāʾ with fatḥa as a purpose particle, yielding “so that a soul may consider.”

ALUSI-FULL:v28p60/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v28p60/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v28p60/r8.claim: The repeated command to fear God may emphasize the first command, or distinguish fulfilling obligations from avoiding prohibitions.

ALUSI-FULL:v28p60/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v28p60/r9.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v28p60/r9.claim: Al-Ālūsī initially favors the distinction: the first taqwā concerns required actions and the second avoiding forbidden acts, with the warning supporting the latter.

ELMALILI:59:18/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:59:18/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:59:18/r1.claim: Believers must seek God’s protection from hypocrisy, disbelief, injustice, and the evil end brought by Satan, obeying His commands and prohibitions.

ELMALILI:59:18/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:59:18/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:59:18/r2.claim: Each person should examine what they have sent ahead for the Day of Resurrection and take account of themselves before being called to account.

ELMALILI:59:18/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:59:18/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:59:18/r3.claim: One explanation calls the Judgment Day “tomorrow” to make it feel as near as tomorrow and spur preparation.

ELMALILI:59:18/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:59:18/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:59:18/r4.claim: A second explanation sees earthly life and the hereafter as two divine days: this world is today and the afterlife tomorrow.

ELMALILI:59:18/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:59:18/r5.speaker: author
ELMALILI:59:18/r5.claim: The verse also urges people each day to consider what they have done for the coming day.

ELMALILI:59:18/r6.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:59:18/r6.speaker: author
ELMALILI:59:18/r6.claim: The repeated command to fear God is not redundant: the first stresses loving obedience and fulfilling duties, while the second stresses fearing and avoiding forbidden acts.

ELMALILI:59:18/r7.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:59:18/r7.speaker: author
ELMALILI:59:18/r7.claim: God knows all deeds and will accordingly recompense people with punishment or reward.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v28p110/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v28p110/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v28p110/r2.claim: After recalling the bloodless victory over Banu al-Naḍir, the failed hopes of their hypocrite allies, and the fate of earlier towns, the surah commands piety as gratitude for God’s favors and promises.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v28p110/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v28p110/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v28p110/r3.claim: Because worldly favors have just been recalled, believers are told to prepare for the afterlife by reflecting on what each self has sent ahead.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v28p110/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v28p110/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v28p110/r4.claim: “Let every soul consider” coordinates one command with another and interrupts the two commands to fear God; explicit “soul” replaces an expected “you” to make the address universal.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v28p110/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v28p110/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v28p110/r5.claim: The indefinite soul in a command means every soul, as in the Quranic conditional “if any of the polytheists seeks your protection” and al-Hariri’s verse.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v28p111/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v28p111/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v28p111/r1.claim: “Tomorrow” metaphorically names the future, bringing a distant time near because tomorrow is the next day; Arab usage and the verses of Qirad b. Ajdaʿ and Zuhayr illustrate it.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v28p111/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v28p111/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v28p111/r2.claim: The indefinite “tomorrow” magnifies and makes the Day’s unknowable reality awe-inspiring.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v28p111/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v28p111/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v28p111/r3.claim: The lām in “for tomorrow” states purpose: deeds are sent ahead for the sake and benefit of the Resurrection day.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v28p111/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v28p111/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v28p111/r4.claim: “Sending ahead” metaphorically describes present work done for future benefit, like preparing a home before travelers or sending a scout before an army; the opposite is leaving work undone.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v28p111/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v28p111/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v28p111/r5.claim: Repeating “fear God” reconnects the rationale after the intervening clause and intensifies the emphasis; conjunction makes the repeated command sound newly established.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v28p111/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v28p111/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v28p111/r6.claim: “God is fully aware of what you do” explains the call to piety, with inna functioning as a causal marker.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v28p112/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v28p112/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v28p112/r1.claim: The first command to fear God can mean fear that motivates action; the second can mean persist in that piety, with God’s awareness measuring their effort.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v28p112/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v28p112/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v28p112/r2.claim: The warning not to forget God addresses those who initially adopted Islam but later neglected piety, especially hypocrites, as in the description of hypocrites as transgressors.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v28p112/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v28p112/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v28p112/r3.claim: Naming God explicitly instead of using a pronoun makes the sentence fully independent like a maxim and cultivates awe in the audience.

TABATABAI:59:18-24#2/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:59:18-24#2/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:59:18-24#2/r1.claim: The warning about those who forgot God reinforces the preceding call: send righteous deeds ahead for judgment, deeds through which the self truly lives.

TABATABAI:59:18-24#3/r10.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:59:18-24#3/r10.speaker: author
TABATABAI:59:18-24#3/r10.claim: The author points readers to earlier reports on remembering God, including those discussed under 2:152 and 33:41.

TABATABAI:59:18-24#3/r8.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:59:18-24#3/r8.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم
TABATABAI:59:18-24#3/r8.claim: A well-known prophetic saying urges people to account for themselves before being held to account, weigh themselves before being weighed, and prepare for the great presentation.

TABATABAI:59:18-24#3/r9.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:59:18-24#3/r9.speaker: أبو الحسن الماضي عليه السلام
TABATABAI:59:18-24#3/r9.claim: A daily self-accounting report says that whoever does good should increase gratitude to God, and whoever does evil should seek God's forgiveness and repent.

TABATABAI:59:18-24/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:59:18-24/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:59:18-24/r1.claim: The author links the coming return to God with 70:6–7, where people regard it as distant while God sees it as near.

TABATABAI:59:18-24/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:59:18-24/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:59:18-24/r2.claim: The first command to fear God means obeying all commands and avoiding all prohibitions; each person should inspect what deeds are being presented for judgment and whether good deeds are accepted.

TABATABAI:59:18-24/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:59:18-24/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:59:18-24/r3.claim: The repeated command concerns care within deeds already performed: repair them, make them sincere for God, and protect them from corruption; the first command governs doing deeds, the second their quality.

TABATABAI:59:18-24/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:59:18-24/r4.speaker: بعضهم
TABATABAI:59:18-24/r4.claim: Some say the first command is repentance for past sins and the second avoidance of future sins; the author rejects this distinction.

TABATABAI:59:18-24/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:59:18-24/r5.speaker: قيل
TABATABAI:59:18-24/r5.claim: Other explanations make the first command about fulfilling obligations and the second about avoiding prohibitions, or treat the second as mere emphasis; the author rejects both.

TABATABAI:59:18/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:59:18/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:59:18/r1.claim: The passage concludes the chapter's account of Banu al-Nadir's breach and worldly and otherworldly loss, compounded by hypocrites urging opposition to God and His Messenger; their root failure was forgetting God and thereby losing sight of their own good.

TABATABAI:59:18/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:59:18/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:59:18/r2.claim: Believers should remember God and examine what they have sent ahead for the return and judgment, since deeds are preserved and bring an inescapable recompense.

TABATABAI:59:18/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:59:18/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:59:18/r3.claim: The verse calls for ongoing watchfulness that deeds be sound and sincere, followed by self-accounting: thank God for good, rebuke oneself for sins, and seek forgiveness.

TABATABAI:59:18/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:59:18/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:59:18/r4.claim: Remembering God through the beautiful names and attributes taught in the Quran is the sole path to complete servitude, the highest human perfection.

TABATABAI:59:18/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:59:18/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:59:18/r5.claim: A human is wholly owned by God and has no independent aspect; perfection means recognizing this dependence, embodying humility and need, and acting according to God's will without heedlessness.

TABATABAI:59:18/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:59:18/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:59:18/r6.claim: Only inward awareness of God, who witnesses and encompasses everything, lets a person view self, attributes, and actions as wholly dependent; then the heart finds reassurance.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p238/r4.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p238/r4.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p238/r4.claim: The closing passage warns believers, especially hypocrites, to remember Judgment Day: forgetting God means forgetting life's purpose and fate, and only Paradise's inhabitants attain true success.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p238/r5.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p238/r5.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p238/r5.claim: Truth has been fully revealed, so continued denial is stubbornness; the Qur'an would shatter a mountain with awe, and unresponsive hearts reveal their own hardness rather than any fault in the Qur'an.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p258/r5.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p258/r5.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p258/r5.claim: Although the closing passage addresses Muslims generally, its context directs it especially to the hypocrites discussed from the sūrah's beginning.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p258/r6.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p258/r6.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p258/r6.claim: Its central warning is to examine one's preparation for the imminent Day of Accountability, knowing that God sees every deed and will recompense it.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p260/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p260/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p260/r1.claim: Though phrased for all believers, the verse is aimed primarily at the hypocrites whose weaknesses the sūrah has exposed.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p260/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p260/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p260/r2.claim: The fundamental remedy for spiritual, intellectual, and moral illness is attention to the reality of accountability; believers must assess their deeds for the coming Judgement.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p260/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p260/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p260/r3.claim: The command to fear God counters the idea that worldly amusement simply ends; this life is followed by certain reward and punishment.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p260/r4.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p260/r4.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p260/r4.claim: “Tomorrow” signifies the Hereafter's nearness and certainty, so people must not defer self-accountability.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p260/r5.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p260/r5.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p260/r5.claim: Repeating the command to fear God emphasizes its importance and reminds people that God knows every word and deed and will repay them.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:59:18/r2.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:59:18/r2.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:59:18/r2.claim: This is the Qur'an's only use of gad as “tomorrow”; the indefinite word makes Judgment seem near while stressing its importance, terror, and unknowable nature.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:59:18/r3.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:59:18/r3.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:59:18/r3.claim: The indefinite nafs means each responsible person must individually take account of what they have prepared.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:59:18/r4.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:59:18/r4.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:59:18/r4.claim: The primary meaning is preparation for the afterlife and self-accounting; planning earthly life according to one's purpose is included.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:59:18/r5.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:59:18/r5.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:59:18/r5.claim: In light of God's forgiveness and acceptance of sincere repentance, even someone with past failings should repent sincerely and use remaining time well.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:59:18/r6.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:59:18/r6.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:59:18/r6.claim: Organizations, though not persons, should periodically assess their goals, resources, results, and future plans; individuals and societies likewise should review whether they live according to their purpose.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:59:18/r7.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:59:18/r7.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:59:18/r7.claim: Because life can end at any moment, self-accounting should not be limited to fixed intervals; illness, nearby deaths, Friday, and Laylat al-Qadr serve as reminders.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:59:18/r8.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:59:18/r8.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:59:18/r8.claim: The second occurrence of “being mindful” emphasizes the first; the first can mean loving obedience, the second careful avoidance of prohibitions.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:59:18/r9.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:59:18/r9.speaker: İbn Âşûr
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:59:18/r9.claim: Another explanation of the second command is to preserve the state already described and remain constant in piety.

STUDYQURAN:59:18/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:59:18/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:59:18/r1.claim: Everyone should reflect on their deeds and assess how they will fare on the Day of Judgment.

STUDYQURAN:59:18/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:59:18/r2.speaker: the Prophet
STUDYQURAN:59:18/r2.claim: Seeing some Muslims in poverty, the Prophet gathered people and recited 4:1 followed by this verse; many then brought food and clothing for the poor.
